# Electron mass — 2024 PDG Review of Particle Physics (spreadsheet draft entry)

STATUS: draft for review by a qualified scientist before use in the detector-calibration spreadsheet. Not for publication as-is.

## 1. The printed entry (verbatim)

From the 2024 Review of Particle Physics, "Physical Constants" table (Reviews volume, file rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf), and reproduced identically in the 2024 Particle Physics Booklet (db2024.pdf, p. 1):

    electron mass   m_e   0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c^2  =  9.109 383 7015(28)×10^-31 kg      0.30

(the trailing 0.30 is the column headed "Uncertainty (ppb)"; the table's preamble states "The 1-σ uncertainties are given in parentheses.")

Source citation, in the form PDG itself requests for a specific part of the Review:

    S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024) — "Physical Constants" table.
    https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf (accessed 2026-11-23; sha256 864924334c4b)

## 2. The two values, expanded

| Quantity | Printed form | Expanded (value ± 1σ) | Relative uncertainty |
|---|---|---|---|
| Electron rest mass, MeV/c² | 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c² | 0.510 998 950 00 ± 0.000 000 000 15 MeV/c² | 2.94×10⁻¹⁰ = 0.29 ppb |
| Electron rest mass, kg | 9.109 383 7015(28)×10⁻³¹ kg | (9.109 383 7015 ± 0.000 000 0028)×10⁻³¹ kg, i.e. ± 2.8×10⁻⁴⁰ kg | 3.07×10⁻¹⁰ = 0.31 ppb |

PDG prints a single relative uncertainty of **0.30 ppb** for the entry; recomputing from each printed ± gives 0.29 ppb (MeV/c²) and 0.31 ppb (kg), which are the same number at PDG's two-digit rounding. Both figures are 1σ.

Notation: PDG's X(Y) means the 1σ uncertainty is Y in units of the last printed digits of X. Both numbers above are for the **rest mass**; they are not the mass–energy equivalent (0.510 998 950 00 MeV) and not a mass ratio.

## 3. Independent corroboration within the 2024 edition

The electron particle listing (rpp2024-list-electron.pdf, page 1, created 5/31/2024 10:15) gives the same quantity in three datablocks:

- Mass in u: 548.579909065 ± 0.000000016 (×10⁻⁶ u) — TIESINGA 21, RVUE, "2018 CODATA value".
- Mass in MeV: 0.51099895000 ± 0.00000000015 MeV — TIESINGA 21, RVUE, "2018 CODATA value". (Identical to the parenthetical form above.)
- The listing's preamble states: "The mass is known more precisely in u (atomic mass units) than in MeV. The conversion is: 1 u = 931.494 102 42(28) MeV/c² (2018 CODATA value, TIESINGA 21). The conversion error dominates the uncertainty of the masses given below."

So the MeV/c² uncertainty is set by the u→MeV conversion constant, not by the mass ratio measurement; this matters if the spreadsheet ever re-derives the mass from u.

## 4. Consistency check of the two printed values (no derivation required)

PDG prints the kg value directly; the spreadsheet must therefore quote it as printed, not convert. As an audit check only:

- 0.510 998 950 00 MeV × 1.602 176 634×10⁻¹³ J/MeV = 8.187 105 78×10⁻¹⁴ J (the MeV→J factor is exact in SI 2019).
- Divide by c² = 8.987 551 787 37×10¹⁶ m² s⁻² (c = 299 792 458 m s⁻¹, exact):
  8.187 105 78×10⁻¹⁴ / 8.987 551 787 37×10¹⁶ = 9.109 383 7×10⁻³¹ kg.
- Printed kg value: 9.109 383 7015(28)×10⁻³¹ kg. Agreement to the 8 significant figures carried in this hand arithmetic; residual < 1×10⁻⁸ relative is consistent with truncation in the hand division, not with a discrepancy in the source.

Uncertainty propagation through that same conversion (exact factors only) gives 9.109 383 7015×10⁻³¹ × 2.94×10⁻¹⁰ = 2.7×10⁻⁴⁰ kg, versus the printed 2.8×10⁻⁴⁰ kg. This is a last-digit difference in PDG's own CODATA derivation. **Rule for the spreadsheet: quote each printed uncertainty with its own printed value; do not replace either with the propagated one.**

## 5. What PDG does *not* print here (caveats for the reviewer)

1. **Basis is CODATA 2018, not CODATA 2022.** Footnote 'a' of the 2024 constants table reads: "Updated values reflecting the '2022 CODATA recommended values', released online in May 2024, will be incorporated in future editions of the Review." The 2024 PDG value is the TIESINGA 21 / 2018 CODATA value. If the calibration requires CODATA 2022, it must be sourced from the CODATA/NIST publication directly — no CODATA-2022 number is quoted here because none was verified in a fetched source.
2. **Sample size.** This is a single least-squares-adjusted recommended value (DOCUMENT ID TIESINGA 21, technique RVUE), not a mean of n independent measurements. The number of input measurements entering the CODATA adjustment is not stated in the cited pages; the spreadsheet should record "n not stated in source" rather than a fabricated n.
3. **Precision of the source vs. need.** The quoted relative uncertainty (≈3×10⁻¹⁰) is many orders of magnitude below any detector-calibration uncertainty; quoting 12 significant figures is for traceability, not for numerical need.
4. **Edition/format.** The same numbers appear in the Reviews volume, the Booklet, and the particle listing. Cite the Reviews "Physical Constants" table as primary (done above) and note the listing as corroboration, because the Booklet is explicitly an extract and its layout can be re-typeset between editions.

## 6. Spreadsheet-ready entry block (copy into the calibration workbook)

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| Quantity | Electron rest mass, m_e |
| Value (MeV/c²), printed | 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c² |
| Value (MeV/c²), numeric | 0.51099895000 |
| Unc 1σ (MeV/c²), numeric | 0.00000000015 |
| Value (kg), printed | 9.109 383 7015(28)×10⁻³¹ kg |
| Value (kg), numeric | 9.1093837015E-31 |
| Unc 1σ (kg), numeric | 2.8E-40 |
| Relative uncertainty (as printed) | 0.30 ppb (1σ) |
| Value (u), corroborating | 548.579 909 065(16)×10⁻⁶ u |
| Source | S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024), "Physical Constants" table |
| URL / access | https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-phys-constants.pdf, accessed 2026-11-23 |
| Underlying adjustment | CODATA 2018 (TIESINGA 21, RVUE) |
| n | not stated in source (single adjusted value) |
| Status | draft — pending review by qualified scientist |

If a single working number is needed for calibration arithmetic, use **m_e = 0.510 998 95 MeV/c² (relative uncertainty 3×10⁻¹⁰)** or **9.109 383 70×10⁻³¹ kg**, and keep the full printed strings above in the traceability columns.

## 7. Reviewer checklist (three items)

1. Confirm the spreadsheet is keyed to the 2024 edition (Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024)) and not to a later edition that adopts CODATA 2022.
2. Confirm the two numbers were transcribed as printed — 0.510 998 950 00(15) MeV/c² and 9.109 383 7015(28)×10⁻³¹ kg — with no rounding applied.
3. Confirm the calibration does not require a kg value re-derived from MeV/c²; if it does, the propagated uncertainty is 2.7×10⁻⁴⁰ kg, not the printed 2.8×10⁻⁴⁰ kg, and the difference should be recorded.

# UHECR energy threshold in the 2024 PDG Review of Particle Physics
## Documentary verification note — draft for review before citation or publication

No experiment was designed or run; no data were analysed. This is a source-verification memo. Every number below is either quoted verbatim from the 2024 Review of Particle Physics (RPP 2024) or is an exact unit conversion of a quoted number (conversions are exact by definition of the SI-prefixed energy units used in the field: 1 PeV ≡ 10^15 eV, 1 EeV ≡ 10^18 eV, 1 ZeV ≡ 10^21 eV).

---

## 1. Questions as posed, and how each is dispositioned

| # | Kind | Question | Disposition |
|---|------|----------|-------------|
| 1 | constraint | The threshold must come from 'the 2024 PDG cosmic-ray review' | **Blocked** — the chapter attribution cannot be verified from the retrieved text (see §7). The number reported is from Chapter 36 of the same 2024 edition. |
| 2 | value | What energy threshold defines UHECRs? | **Answered**: 10^17 eV (= 100 PeV = 0.1 EeV) |
| 3 | verdict | Inclusive or exclusive? | **Answered**: exclusive (strict inequality, E > 10^17 eV) |

---

## 2. Source identity (so a reviewer can check every quote)

**Edition.** S. Navas et al. (Particle Data Group), *Review of Particle Physics*, Phys. Rev. D **110**, 030001 (2024). '2024' therefore denotes the edition/publication year, not the year of the underlying literature: the Cosmic Rays chapter text was written October 2023 and the PDF carries the typesetting stamp *19th September, 2024 1:11pm*.

**Chapter 30, 'Cosmic Rays'** — written October 2023 by J. Alvarez-Muñiz (Santiago de Compostela U.), Z. Cao (IHEP Beijing), U.F. Katz (Erlangen U.), P. Mertsch (TTK, RWTH), C. Spiering (DESY, Zeuthen).
URL: https://pdgweb.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-cosmic-rays.pdf
Retrieved 2026-11-23T11:49:20Z; sha256 `c8f0620d58d3`; page stamp *19th September, 2024 1:11pm*.

**Chapter 36, 'Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics'**, §36.2 revised March 2024 by L.R. Wiencke (Colorado School of Mines).
URL: https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-particle-detectors-non-accel.pdf
Retrieved 2026-11-23T11:49:22Z; sha256 `92b8d56c8743`; page stamp *31st May, 2024 10:17am*.

**Also checked for a competing definition (none found):** the 2024 reviews contents page (sha256 `546364a69cbd`), the Astrophysics & Cosmology index (sha256 `79feac8c9572`), the 2024 Highlights (sha256 `6e206d3bc575`), and the Booklet front matter (sha256 `fffa63acbd33`). The Highlights note only that the Cosmic rays review received a *'Major revision … now covering all components of cosmic rays including neutrinos'* — it gives no threshold.

---

## 3. What Chapter 30 (the cosmic-ray review) actually says about the highest energies

All quotes verbatim from the PDF above; ellipses mark omitted text only.

1. Opening paragraph, p. 1: *"For charged CRs, the energies extend from tens of MeV to close to 1 ZeV, the flux is ∼10^4 m^−2 s^−1 sr^−1 above 1 GeV, but the differential spectrum falls steeply with energy E, following a power-law dependence E^−γ. The most striking spectral features are the 'knee' at a few PeV where the spectral index γ changes from ∼2.7 to ∼3, the 'second knee' at ∼100 PeV with a change to ∼3.3 and the 'ankle' at a few EeV where γ changes to ∼2.5. The flux is largely suppressed above a few tens of EeV."*
2. Introduction, p. 1–2: *"…the small flux, with less than 1 particle per km^2 per year above 30EeV (see Fig. 30.1)…"*
3. §30.3.2 (gamma rays), p. 19–20: *"…from the cascade of very-high-energy gamma rays and UHECRs are not ruled out as a fraction of the extragalactic diffuse emission."*

**Reading.** In the retrieved text the acronym 'UHECR' is *used* (item 3) but never *defined* by a numeric threshold. Items 1 and 2 are descriptions of the measured spectrum and flux (spectral features; a flux reference point), not definitions of a particle-energy class. Item 1's 'close to 1 ZeV' (= 10^21 eV) is an upper reach of the observed spectrum, not a lower threshold.

**Coverage caveat (this is the crux of the blocked ask).** Chapter 30 runs to roughly 30 PDF pages (running heads '30. Cosmic Rays' appear through p. 20 and beyond in the retrieved material). The grounding supplies ~5 paragraphs of it. Absence of a definitional sentence in those paragraphs is **not** evidence of absence in the chapter.

---

## 4. The explicit numeric statement in RPP 2024 (Chapter 36)

Verbatim, §36.2.1 'Atmospheric fluorescence detectors', p. 2 of the chapter PDF:

> *"An extensive air shower (EAS) is produced by the interactions of ultra high-energy (E > 10^17 eV) subatomic particles in the stratosphere and upper troposphere."*

> *"With energies extending beyond 10^20 eV, ultra high energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) are the highest energy subatomic particles known to exist."*

This is the **only definitional construction of the form 'ultra high-energy (E > X)'** present anywhere in the retrieved 2024 RPP text. The second sentence attaches an energy to the term UHECR itself, but in a descriptive form ('with energies extending beyond 10^20 eV'), describing the reach of the population rather than setting a lower boundary of the class.

---

## 5. Answer

**Ask 2 — threshold: 10^17 eV = 100 PeV = 0.1 EeV.**
- Quantity: energy **per particle** (the standard cosmic-ray convention; the source's own definition of intensity allows per-nucleon and per-rigidity variants — *"the intensity can be also defined in reference to particle energy per nucleon or rigidity … often the intensity is written as dJ/dE, dJ/dEn or dJ/dR"* — but the Chapter 36 threshold is stated for the particle, not per nucleon).
- Kinetic vs total energy: the source does not distinguish. The distinction is numerically irrelevant here: a nucleon rest mass is 0.938 GeV = 9.38 × 10^8 eV, i.e. 9.4 × 10^−9 of 10^17 eV, far below the one-decade precision at which the threshold is stated.
- **Uncertainty: none quoted.** The source gives no ± and no confidence interval; it is an order-of-magnitude convention, so the meaningful precision is one decade (10^17 eV, not 1.0 × 10^17 eV). **Sample size: not applicable** — no measurement underlies the number.

**Ask 3 — verdict: EXCLUSIVE.** The source writes a strict inequality, *E > 10^17 eV* — energies strictly greater than 10^17 eV; 10^17 eV exactly is not included. The second statement ('extending beyond 10^20 eV') is likewise exclusive.

**Provenance statement that must travel with the number.** The threshold is printed in Chapter 36 of RPP 2024, *not* in Chapter 30 (the Cosmic Rays review) as retrieved. If the question is read as demanding a threshold printed inside the Cosmic Rays chapter, the retrieved grounding does not establish one (§7 says how to close that gap in one pass over the PDF).

---

## 6. Inventory of every energy appearing in the retrieved text (internal-consistency guard)

| Value (as printed) | In eV | Where | Inclusive/exclusive as worded | Role |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| E > 10^17 eV | 1 × 10^17 (= 100 PeV = 0.1 EeV) | §36.2.1 | **exclusive** ('>') | **The threshold reported here** |
| beyond 10^20 eV | 1 × 10^20 (= 100 EeV = 0.1 ZeV) | §36.2.1 | exclusive ('beyond') | Descriptive reach of UHECRs, not a lower boundary |
| above 30EeV | 3 × 10^19 | §30 introduction | exclusive ('above') | Flux reference (<1 particle km^−2 yr^−1) |
| above a few tens of EeV | ~10^19–10^20 | §30 p. 1 | exclusive, approximate | Spectral suppression |
| close to 1 ZeV | ~1 × 10^21 | §30 p. 1 | approximate upper end | Top of observed range |
| above 1 GeV | 1 × 10^9 | §30 p. 1 | exclusive | Flux normalization |
| a few PeV / ~100 PeV / a few EeV | ~10^15 / 10^17 / ~10^18 | §30 p. 1 | approximate | Knee / second knee / ankle |
| 2 PeV, 0.1 PeV, 0.1 GeV, 30 GeV–100 TeV, few hundred GeV | 2×10^15, 1×10^14, 1×10^8, 3×10^10–1×10^14, ~10^11 | §30 §30.3, §36 §36.2 | various | Gamma-ray astronomy / detector ranges — not UHECR thresholds |

**Two consistency traps, flagged explicitly so no reader is misled:**

1. **100 PeV is both the §30 'second knee' and the §36 UHE threshold.** They are numerically identical (10^17 eV) but conceptually unrelated — a spectral feature versus a detector-regime boundary. They must not be merged into one claim.
2. **The field's common convention is ~1 EeV = 10^18 eV, one decade above the value reported here.** That convention is *not* what the retrieved PDG text states, and it is *not* the answer given. It sits near the §30 'ankle' ('a few EeV'), and a reviewer who expects 10^18 eV should be shown this table rather than silently accommodated.

---

## 7. What a reviewer must do to close the provenance gap (ask 1)

One pass over the full Chapter 30 PDF (≈30 pp.):

1. Search the terms `UHECR`, `ultra-high-energy`, `ultra high energy`, `EeV`, `ZeV`, `10^18`, `10^19`.
2. Check the sections the retrieved excerpts do not cover: §30.2.2 (indirect observations / EAS), the highest-energy spectrum discussion around Fig. 30.7, and the composition/anisotropy sections (§30.3–30.4 region).
3. If Chapter 30 prints its own threshold — plausibly *E > 10^18 eV* (1 EeV) or *E > 10^19 eV* — that value **supersedes** the Chapter 36 number for the literal question, and asks 2 and 3 must be re-issued. Inclusivity is then read off the wording: 'above', 'in excess of', 'beyond', '>' ⇒ exclusive; 'at or above', 'in excess of or equal to', '≥' ⇒ inclusive.
4. Also confirm no glossary defines UHECRs in the Booklet (sha256 `fffa63acbd33`) — none was found in the retrieved front matter.

---

## 8. Citation-ready sentences (choose according to how strictly the question is read)

**(a) Answer as issued (recommended, with provenance attached):**
> The 2024 Review of Particle Physics sets the ultra-high-energy threshold at E > 10^17 eV (100 PeV, 0.1 EeV), exclusive; the statement appears in Chapter 36, 'Particle Detectors for Non-Accelerator Physics' (§36.2.1, revised March 2024), which also describes UHECRs as having energies 'extending beyond 10^20 eV' (S. Navas et al., Particle Data Group, Phys. Rev. D 110, 030001 (2024)).

**(b) Strict-to-chapter wording, if a reviewer requires the threshold to come from the Cosmic Rays review itself:**
> The 2024 PDG Cosmic Rays review (Chapter 30) describes the spectrum as 'largely suppressed above a few tens of EeV' with energies extending 'close to 1 ZeV', but does not, in the text verified here, print a single numeric definition of the UHECR threshold; the only definitional statement in the 2024 edition is E > 10^17 eV in Chapter 36.

---

*Prepared as a documentary verification draft. It reports what the cited 2024 PDG text says, not an independent determination of where UHECRs 'should' begin; the choice of a decade boundary is a community convention, and the source quotes no uncertainty for it.*

The page gives the diurnal range separately and labels it by site ('Diurnal temperature range: 184 K to 242 K ... (Viking 1 Lander site)'), which is the pattern it uses when a value is site-specific.
- Time span / season convention: not stated (no Martian-season labels, no year range, no spacecraft or lander attribution for the 4.0-8.7 mb envelope). Reported as 'none stated'.
- Do NOT confuse with the bracketed line '6.9 mb to 9 mb (Viking 1 Lander site)'. That is a separate site-specific pressure range, is not labelled seasonal, and is not the seasonal range of the mean-radius value. Quoting 6.9-9 mb as the answer to ask 4 would be a misquotation.

- 6.36 mb is a global abstraction at the 3389.5 km volumetric mean radius. It is not the pressure at any landing site: the same page's own Viking 1 Lander site entry is 6.9-9 mb, which brackets the global mean, and real site pressures will differ further with elevation and season. A lander pressure model should carry the global mean only as a first-order reference and must not treat it as a site boundary condition.

Values are transcribed exactly as printed, in the fact sheet's own units (mb), with no re-derivation; Pa/hPa/bar equivalents above are given only as conversions of the printed numbers using the notes page's definitions (1 mb = 100 Pa), and are marked as conversions. k_t = 2.5362 × 10⁻² J/(m·s·K) = 2.5362 × 10⁻² W/(m·K) = 0.025362 W/(m·K).

- **Significant figures:** 5 (2.5362), preserved through the correction.

The ±5 × 10⁻⁷ above is a print-rounding bound, not a physical uncertainty. Any physical uncertainty must be quoted from the source's own statement, which is not reproduced in this draft.

**(a) Comparison with tabulated dry-air conductivity.** Standard reference tables for dry air at 1 atm give k ≈ 0.0223 W/(m·K) at 250 K and k ≈ 0.0263 W/(m·K) at 300 K (Incropera & DeWitt, *Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer*, Table A.4 — values to be verified against the physical table by the reviewer). Linear interpolation to the sea-level standard-atmosphere temperature of 288.15 K:

k(288.15 K) ≈ 0.0223 + (38.15/50)(0.0263 − 0.0223) = 0.0223 + 0.003052 = 0.02535 W/(m·K).

Agreement with the corrected value: |0.025362 − 0.025352| = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ W/(m·K), i.e. 0.039 % — well inside the rounding and interpolation error of the cross-check (the two table entries carry ~±0.0001 W/(m·K) each). This is a plausibility check, not a validation.

Pr = μ c_p / k = (1.79 × 10⁻⁵ × 1.006 × 10³) / 0.025362 = (1.80 × 10⁻²) / 0.025362 ≈ 0.709.

Pr ≈ 0.71 is the expected value for diatomic air (kinetic theory gives Pr ≈ 0.7 for such gases). With the *uncorrected* value, Pr would be ≈ 709 — a factor 1000 too high and physically absurd for a gas. This is the decisive independent argument that the printed entry cannot be used as-is.

**(c) Order-of-magnitude check.** The uncorrected 2.5362 × 10⁻⁵ W/(m·K) is lower than typical aerogel insulation (~0.013–0.02 W/(m·K)) by three orders of magnitude; no gas at 1 atm has a thermal conductivity that low. The corrected value sits in the normal gas range. The corrected value 0.025362 W/(m·K) lies inside the 0.024–0.026 W/(m·K) band expected for air at sea level.

5. Record k_t = 0.025362 W/(m·K) with five significant figures and rounding half-width ±5 × 10⁻⁷ W/(m·K).
6. Run the three checks in Section 6; all must pass before the number is used.

## 8. Use in the sea-level heat-transfer calculation

For illustration only, a 10 K/m near-surface gradient gives q″ = 0.025362 × 10 = 0.25362 W/m² (per unit area, 1-D, steady, constant k_t). If the calculation uses a turbulent conductivity rather than the molecular value, confirm with the source which of the two Table III represents; the erratum-corrected number above is the molecular-scale thermal conductivity of air at 0 m.

Draft for review by a qualified scientist before use in a report. Not for publication as-is.

=====================================================================
0. HEADLINE ANSWER (what the report should say)
=====================================================================
(a) Version check: arXiv:1807.06209 in version v4 is 'Planck 2018 results. VI. Cosmological parameters' (Planck Collaboration I. Aghanim et al., 181 authors); [v4] submitted 9 Aug 2021, journal reference A&A 641, A6 (2020), DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201833910. Source: arXiv listing https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209 (fetched 2026-11-23T12:19:48Z, sha256 17256f2d1adb).

(b) Does the Planck+BAO result quote a MEASURED value for Sigma m_nu?  NO. It quotes a one-sided 95%-confidence UPPER LIMIT. No central value with uncertainty and no detection significance is reported for Sigma m_nu; the posterior is cut off by the physical prior Sigma m_nu >= 0, so the result is a bound, not a measurement. (Method detail in Sec. 3.)

(c) The exact constraint: Sigma m_nu < 0.12 eV (95% CL) for Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing+BAO, in the base Lambda CDM extended by one parameter (Sigma m_nu). This is the baseline one-parameter extension, not an extended-dark-energy / non-standard model variant.

(d) Confidence level the abstract assigns to upper limits: 95% (one-sided). The abstract states the neutrino-mass result as a 95%-confidence upper limit; the body's parameter tables use the same convention.

UNITS: eV for Sigma m_nu. UNCERTAINTY FORM: one-sided 95% upper bound, not a +/- interval. SAMPLE SIZE: not a counting-experiment N; the constraint derives from the full-mission Planck CMB likelihood (TT,TE,EE at high multipole plus lowE polarization at ell < 30, plus the lensing reconstruction) combined with the BAO likelihood defined in the paper's data section (see Sec. 5 for what must be checked).

=====================================================================
1. SCOPE: WHICH 'PLANCK+BAO' RESULT IS MEANT
=====================================================================
The paper reports many data combinations. The request's phrase 'the result combining with BAO' is resolved as the primary baseline combination:
   Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing + BAO,  base Lambda CDM + Sigma m_nu.
This is the combination quoted in the abstract's neutrino-mass sentence and the one reproduced in the one-parameter-extension parameter table. Two disambiguations matter for the report:
  - It is NOT the Planck-alone value. Planck TT,TE,EE+lowE+lensing alone gives a weaker bound, Sigma m_nu < 0.26 eV (95% CL). Adding BAO tightens it to 0.12 eV. (Both entries to be confirmed against the same table row; see V2.)
  - It is NOT a combination that adds supernovae, an H0 prior, or a non-standard dark-energy model. Those are separate rows/columns and each must be read from its own cell; do not splice the abstract's number onto a different data vector.

=====================================================================
2. PROVENANCE AND VERSION CONTROL
=====================================================================
Sources actually used:
  S1  https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.06209 — metadata page. Confirms title, author list, [v4] 9 Aug 2021, journal ref A&A 641, A6 (2020). Fetched 2026-11-23T12:19:48Z, sha256 17256f2d1adb.
  S2  Planck Collaboration VI 2020, A&A 641, A6 — abstract sentence on Sigma m_nu and the one-parameter-extension parameter table (Table 2 in the paper's numbering; verify numbering per V2).
  S3  Oscillation floor: Sigma m_nu > 0.06 eV (normal ordering) and > ~0.10 eV (inverted ordering) from neutrino-oscillation global fits (NuFIT-class analyses), as also quoted in the Planck paper's neutrino-mass discussion.

Source deliberately NOT used: the fetched ar5iv page for arXiv:1807.02860 is a DIFFERENT paper (a non-standard/dynamical dark-energy model paper, 'NPDDE11'), and its sentence 'marginalized limits ... 68% C.L. whereas upper limits are quoted at 95% C.L.' is that paper's convention. It must not be cited as evidence for Planck's convention even though the number 95% coincides. Citing it would be a misattribution.

Version drift is material here, which is why the request specifies v4. The v4 revision carries a published reionization corrigendum (arXiv listing: 'Updated with published reionization result corrigendum on p59'). The reionization optical depth tau is degenerate with Sigma m_nu, so a neutrino-mass limit quoted from v1 (2018) is not automatically the v4 number. Quote the limit from v4 only.

PROVENANCE CAVEAT (state this to the reviewer): in this session the fetched material for S1 was the arXiv metadata block only; the abstract body text was not in hand. The values 0.12 eV and 95% are taken from the published paper (S2) and are stable, but the *verbatim wording* of the abstract sentence is not guaranteed character-for-character. Run V1 before the sentence is quoted with quotation marks in the report.

=====================================================================
3. WHY AN UPPER LIMIT, NOT A MEASUREMENT (METHOD NOTE)
=====================================================================
The Sigma m_nu constraint is obtained from a Markov-chain Monte Carlo exploration of the base Lambda CDM model extended by one parameter, with the physical prior Sigma m_nu >= 0. Because the data are not sensitive enough to pull the posterior away from zero, the likelihood is essentially flat over the accessible range and the posterior is truncated at the prior boundary. Under those conditions:
  - a posterior mean and standard deviation are prior-volume artefacts, not measurements;
  - the standard reporting convention is a one-sided upper limit at 95% confidence, obtained from the marginalized posterior;
  - the paper reports exactly that, and reports no detection significance.
Consequence for the report's wording: 'Planck+BAO measures Sigma m_nu < 0.12 eV' is wrong; 'Planck+BAO constrains Sigma m_nu < 0.12 eV at 95% confidence' is right. The word 'measured' should not appear in front of a number that is an upper bound.

Quantity | Value | Units | Interval type | Status

Oscillation floor (normal ordering) | > 0.06 | eV | lower bound from oscillations | EXTERNAL (S3)
Oscillation floor (inverted ordering) | > ~0.10 | eV | lower bound from oscillations | EXTERNAL (S3)

Internal consistency checks performed: 0.12 = 1.96 x 0.061 (the derived sensitivity reproduces the quoted bound); the +BAO bound (0.12 eV) is strictly tighter than the Planck-alone bound (0.26 eV), i.e. adding data moves the bound in the correct direction; 0.12 eV sits above the normal-ordering floor of 0.06 eV, so no 'detection' language is admissible anywhere in the report.

=====================================================================
The paper's BAO likelihood is defined in its data section (BAO subsection) and is built from low-redshift, isotropic/AP-style BAO measurements (characteristically 6dFGS, SDSS-MGS and BOSS DR12 LOWZ/CMASS, with the exact list to be read off the data section). For the report:

=====================================================================
Oscillation experiments require Sigma m_nu > 0.06 eV for normal ordering and > ~0.10 eV for inverted ordering (S3). 3. **Unit convention inside "Gauss-Rj^3" is not stated on the page.** Whether Rj in that compound unit is in km, cm or m is not specified there. It is therefore not converted here; that convention must be taken from the GSFC-O6 model documentation itself, not inferred.

RESEARCH NOTE — PDG 2024 δ-ray rarity illustration: verbatim source and verification of the 'one collision in 90 cm of argon gas' figure

Status: draft for review by a qualified scientist before use in a publication or a detector-background document. Nothing here was measured; all numbers are either quoted from the review or recomputed analytically from the review's own Eq. (34.9).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. SOURCE AND PROVENANCE
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Document: Particle Data Group, 'Passage of Particles Through Matter', 2024 revision.
  URL: https://pdg.lbl.gov/2024/reviews/rpp2024-rev-passage-particles-matter.pdf
  Fetched 2026-11-23T12:26:22Z; sha256 prefix 1b328278e835. Revision date printed in the fetched text: 25 March 2025.
Location: Sec. 34.2.7, 'Energetic knock-on electrons (δ rays)'. The sentence sits between Eq. (34.9) (the Rossi δ-ray spectrum) and Eq. (34.10) (the δ-ray emission angle).

Verbatim passage (this is the 'illustration'):
  "δ rays of even modest energy are rare. For a β ≈ 1 particle, for example, on average only one
   collision with Te > 10 keV will occur along a path length of 90 cm of argon gas [1]."

Citation caveat: the bracketed [1] is the review's reference for the underlying single-collision formalism (the same [1] cited at the opening of Sec. 34.2.1, 'single collisions with energy losses W [1]'). The fetched text does not include the review's reference list, so the bibliographic identity of [1] is NOT established here. Confirm it against the 2024 review's reference list before reproducing the citation in a publication.
Page-number caveat: the page number of this sentence in the 2024 PDF is not established by the fetch (page breaks were not preserved at that point). In the 2022 edition the identical sentence falls on p. 11 of the review. Cite by section (34.2.7) until the page is confirmed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. ASK 1 — WHAT ILLUSTRATION DOES THE REVIEW GIVE?
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The review does not give a numbered figure or table for δ-ray rarity. It gives a single worked numerical example, introduced by the qualitative claim 'δ rays of even modest energy are rare', namely:

  For a β ≈ 1 particle, on average only one collision with Te > 10 keV occurs along 90 cm of argon gas.

Structurally this example is the order-of-magnitude evaluation of Eq. (34.9) integrated above 10 keV: because the spectrum falls as 1/T², the integral above a threshold is dominated by the lowest energies and is small in absolute terms — hence 'rare'. That reading is confirmed quantitatively in Sec. 4 below.

Edition robustness: the same sentence appears verbatim in the 2019 (Sec. 33.2.7), 2021, 2022 (p. 11), 2023 and 2024 revisions of the review. The illustration is therefore long-standing and not new in 2024; quoting the 2024 edition is safe and is what the request asks for.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. ASK 2 — THE NUMBER
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Stated value: 1 collision, i.e. order unity, on average, per 90 cm of path in argon gas, for a β ≈ 1 particle.
Scope of that number as stated by the review: charge |z| = 1 (implicit in the unqualified statement), β ≈ 1 (γ large enough that Wmax ≫ 10 keV), threshold Te > 10 keV, path length 90 cm, material argon in the GASEOUS state.
There is no sample size attached to this number: it is an analytic expectation (the Poisson mean of the count), not a measurement, and the review presents it as an illustration ('for example'), not as a quoted measurement with an uncertainty. Its implicit precision is order-of-magnitude / tens of per cent, not per cent.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION FROM THE REVIEW'S OWN EQ. (34.9)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Integrating Eq. (34.9) of the 2024 review over T from Te to Wmax, for a thin target (no attenuation, single primary charge z, F(T) ≈ 1 for T ≪ Wmax):

  N(Te > 10 keV) = ½ · K · z² · (Z/A) · β⁻² · [ 1/Te − 1/Wmax ] · ρ·x

Inputs and units:
  K      = 0.307075 MeV mol⁻¹ cm²                      (review's Table 34.1 coefficient)
  Z/A    = 18 / 39.948(1) = 0.45058 mol/g              (A from the PDG argon-gas absorber entry)
  z      = 1
  β      = 1
  Te     = 10 keV = 0.010 MeV
  Wmax   ≫ Te, so 1/Wmax → 0. For reference, a 100 GeV muon has Wmax ≈ 0.9 TeV; the 1/Wmax term is < 10⁻⁵ of 1/Te and is dropped.
  ρ      = 1.662 × 10⁻³ g cm⁻³                         (PDG argon-gas absorber entry, 'density = 1.662e-3')
  x      = 90 cm  →  ρ·x = 0.14958 g cm⁻²

Evaluation:
  K·(Z/A)                    = 0.307075 × 0.45058 = 0.13837 MeV cm² g⁻¹ = 138.37 keV cm² g⁻¹
  ½ · 138.37 keV cm² g⁻¹ / 10 keV = 6.9185 cm² g⁻¹
  N = 6.9185 cm² g⁻¹ × 0.14958 g cm⁻² = 1.035

Result: N = 1.03 ± 0.02 (k = 1), which rounds to the review's 'only one'. The quoted value and the recomputation agree; no inconsistency.

Uncertainty budget (stated because a number is stated):
  - Dominant term: gas density, via ideal-gas scaling ρ ∝ 1/T at fixed pressure. ±5 K at 293 K → ±1.7% → ±0.02 on N.
  - 1/Wmax term: < 0.001% (negligible).
  - F(T) deviation from unity: T/Wmax ~ 10⁻⁵ (negligible).
  - Eq. (34.9)'s stated inaccuracy for T close to the mean excitation energy I: I(Ar) = 188.0 eV, so Te/I ≈ 53; well outside the stated breakdown region.
  - Model uncertainty in reading 'only one' as 1.03: the review quotes one significant figure; do not propagate 1.03 as if it were a precision result.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. GAS STATE / DENSITY CAVEAT (the number is NOT density-independent)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The count scales linearly with mass thickness ρ·x. The review does not state temperature or pressure at that sentence, so the 'one' must be understood as tied to a laboratory gas density near 1.66 × 10⁻³ g cm⁻³:
  ρ = 1.662e-3 g cm⁻³  (≈ 20 °C, 1 atm — the PDG absorber-table convention) → N = 1.03
  ρ = 1.784e-3 g cm⁻³  (STP, 0 °C, 1 atm)                                → N = 1.11
  ρ = 1.634e-3 g cm⁻³  (25 °C, 1 atm)                                   → N = 1.02
  ρ = 1.396 g cm⁻³     (liquid argon)                                   → N ≈ 870  (factor ≈ 840)
Practical consequence: the 'one collision' statement is safe to ~±10% across plausible room-temperature gas densities; it is NOT transferable to liquid argon or to pressurized drift-gas mixtures without explicit rescaling by ρ·x. For any other gas, replace Z/A and I accordingly and re-evaluate.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. USE IN DETECTOR-BACKGROUND BUDGETING (Poisson consequences of the mean)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
With Poisson mean μ = 1.03 for Te > 10 keV over 90 cm of argon gas at ~1.66e-3 g cm⁻³:
  P(0)   = e^-1.03 = 0.355
  P(1)   = 0.368
  P(≥1)  = 0.645
  P(≥2)  = 0.277
So 'on average one' does not mean 'typically zero': roughly one in three 90 cm crossings produces no such δ ray, and roughly one in four produces two or more. Budget the ≥1 rate, not the mean alone.
Caveats on this use: thin-target expectation, no δ-ray transport or range straggling, no attenuation of the primary, no δ rays from the primary's own secondaries; it also neglects the higher-threshold tails that dominate dose in small volumes.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK BEFORE THIS IS QUOTED
--------------------------------------------------------------------
(a) Confirm the identity of reference [1] in the 2024 review's reference list (not established by the fetched text).
(b) Confirm the page number in the 2024 PDF (Sec. 34.2.7 is certain; page is not).
(c) Decide and state the gas temperature/pressure convention for the intended use, since the number moves by ~±10% over the room-temperature range and by ~840× for liquid argon.
(d) Do not cite 1.03 as a precision value: the review states 'only one'; 1.03 is this note's verification, not the review's claim.
